summary: A millimetre-scale crust consortium grows over cooled volcanic rock, combining a green photosynthetic layer, mineral-weathering partners and the ancestral nitrogen fixer. Dust and dead tissue gradually accumulate around its margins. Exposed colonies develop red-purple screening, while sheltered ones remain greener (F7, F9, F14, F24, F25).

chains.trait: Adherent mineral-weathering crust with nitrogen-fixing partners
links: Newly cooled volcanic surfaces provide mineral substrate but little organic matter or available nitrogen.
Photosynthetic partners supply carbon while microbial acids weather accessible mineral surfaces.
The ancestral symbiont fixes nitrogen using energy and protected microsites within the consortium.
Crust texture traps dust, and turnover adds organic matter to small rooting pockets.
chains.play: Find the dust-filled margins where later pioneers can establish; compare intact crust with nearby bare rock.
chains.weakness: Colonization requires suitable moisture and a stable cooled surface. Abrasion, trampling, deep burial and prolonged drought interrupt growth.
observe: Fine dust remains lodged along raised crust margins after wind clears nearby rock.
A naturally lifted edge exposes a thin green living layer.
Small grass seedlings occur in accumulated debris beside older crust patches.

plausibility.summary: Acids weather mineral surfaces gradually; the crust does not rapidly split intact basalt. Nitrogen fixation does not remove phosphorus or water limitation, and succession has no universal timetable.

analogues.mechanism: Lichen acids contribute to mineral weathering, while cyanobacterial associations illustrate nitrogen input within a photosynthetic consortium. [Chen and colleagues](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0341-8162(99)00085-5); [Lichen Biology](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/lichen-biology/87CA882464AED46E121E8C79A99B4993).

chains.trait: Red-purple screening above a green photosynthetic layer
links: Exposed rock colonies receive more radiation than shaded fissure colonies, with elevated UV on high slopes.
Excess exposure can damage the photosynthetic layer.
A superficial red-purple pigment layer reduces damaging radiation reaching living cells.
The screen improves exposure tolerance but can reduce useful light and increase heating.
chains.play: Read broad differences in exposure from neighbouring red and green colonies without treating colour as an elevation meter.
chains.weakness: Screening costs carbon and does not prevent overheating or dehydration; heavily screened colonies perform poorly in deep shade.
observe: Sun-facing crust is red-purple beside greener colonies under the same rock lip.
A chipped natural edge shows green beneath the coloured surface.
Hot dry colonies look shrunken despite retaining their red screen.

plausibility.summary: The overlay follows the seeded pigment canon. Earth lichen screens support the mechanism, not an exact pigment identity. Red here signals exposure stress; it does not imply alkaloids or a crater-wide metal anomaly.

analogues.mechanism: Cortical pigments can screen underlying photobionts; their benefits depend on exposure and carbon balance. Primigenia's red-purple chemistry is an extrapolation from this architecture. [Lichen Biology](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/lichen-biology/87CA882464AED46E121E8C79A99B4993).

food_for: Detritivores consuming weathered crust margins and dead microbial tissue

poison.signal: Red-purple exposed surfaces over green tissue indicate radiation screening, without the red-veined alkaloid pattern.

gameplay.notes: A soil-building community rather than a concentrated edible mineral deposit. Substrate contamination can still make a patch hazardous near geothermal seeps. Crater-rim occupancy indicates suitable rock, not the second capsule's purpose.

relations.note: Creates dust-and-litter microsites beside fissures where the grass may establish; mature grass can later shade the crust.
Shares cooled lava terrain where damp nutrient-poor seeps interrupt otherwise dry surfaces.
Consumes softened dead margins and associated decaying material on damp ground.
Can occupy exposed rock near crater vegetation without sharing Hierroflor's nickel specialization.

generator.trunk: None; a tightly attached crust follows the rock surface.

branching.buttress: None; structural branching parameters are inactive.

leaf.arrangement: Contiguous irregular plates with expanding colony margins

overlay_rules: Red-purple screening strengthens on persistently exposed surfaces.
Sheltered margins and naturally exposed inner tissue remain greener.
Dust occupies cracks rather than replacing the living pigment.

placement.slope: Stable rock faces, 0–70 degrees; favour moisture-retaining texture.
placement.wetness: Intermittently damp with drying intervals; not permanently submerged.
placement.soil: Cooled basalt and cohesive tuff with little developed soil; exclude hot active vent surfaces.
placement.fog: Fog wetting favours activity where droplets reach the surface.
placement.density: Discontinuous islands on young rock, merging locally on older suitable surfaces.

generator.seasonal: Growth follows wet periods; dry colonies become metabolically inactive. Alpine patches remain inactive beneath persistent snow.
generator.wind_response: The adherent crust does not sway; airborne grit abrades exposed margins while rough patches retain dust.

journal.en: A red skin on the stone, green underneath. Dust stays where it has taken hold.
journal.es: Una piel roja sobre la piedra, verde por debajo. El polvo se queda donde ha prendido.

changelog.what: flora pass: 7 voices drafted and peer-reviewed, Composer botanical referee, sol chaired and applied the fixes

observe: The red skin follows every hollow in the cooled stone.
Green tissue shows at a naturally broken edge.
Dust gathers where a colony meets a damp fissure.
secrets: The best seedling microsites occur where old crust margins meet water-holding cracks, rather than at the reddest colony centres.
Similar crust on ordinary lava and crater-rim rock prevents its colour from serving as a unique meteor clue.
